title: The Trial
author: Franz Kafka
openingText: Someone must have slandered Josef K., because one morning he was arrested although he had done nothing wrong. The cook employed by Mrs Grubach, his landlady, who brought him breakfast every morning at about eight, did not come this time. That had never happened before. K. waited a little longer, watching from his pillow the old woman who lived opposite and was observing him with a curiosity quite unusual for her; then, both puzzled and hungry, he rang. There was a knock at once, and a man he had never seen in this apartment came in. He was slim but solidly built, and wore a close-fitting black outfit furnished, like a travelling suit, with various pleats, pockets, buckles, buttons and a belt, which made it look particularly practical, although it was not clear what purpose it was meant to serve. “Who are you?” K. asked, immediately sitting half upright in bed. But the man passed over the question, as though his appearance simply had to be accepted, and merely asked in return: “You rang?” “Anna is to bring me my breakfast,” said K., trying at first, in silence, to work out who the man actually was by watching him closely and thinking it over. But the man did not expose himself to this scrutiny for very long; he turned to the door and opened it a little to tell someone apparently standing just behind it: “He wants Anna to bring him his breakfast.” A small burst of laughter came from the next room; it was impossible to tell from the sound whether more than one person had joined in. Although this could not have told the stranger anything he had not already known, he now said to K., in the tone of someone delivering a report: “That is impossible.” “That would be something new,” said K., jumping out of bed and quickly pulling on his trousers. “I want to see what sort of people are in the next room, and how Mrs Grubach intends to account to me for this disturbance.” It immediately occurred to him that he need not have said this aloud and that in doing so he was, in a sense, acknowledging the stranger's right to supervise him, but just now it did not seem important. The stranger did take it that way, however, for he said: “Wouldn't you rather stay here?” “I have no wish either to stay here or to be spoken to by you until you introduce yourself.” “I meant well,” said the stranger, and now opened the door of his own accord. The next room, which K. entered more slowly than he wished, looked at first almost exactly as it had the previous evening. It was Mrs Grubach's living room; perhaps there was a little more space than usual today in this room crammed with furniture, blankets, china and photographs, but it was not immediately apparent, especially since the main change consisted in the presence of a man sitting by the open window with a book, from which he now looked up. “You should have stayed in your room! Didn't Franz tell you?” “Well, what do you want?” said K., looking from his new acquaintance to the man called Franz, who had remained in the doorway, and back again. Through the open window the old woman was visible once more; with the truly aged person's curiosity, she had moved to the window now opposite them so that she could go on seeing everything. “I want Mrs Grubach—” said K., making a movement as though wrenching himself free of the two men, although they were standing well away from him, and preparing to go on. “No,” said the man by the window, throwing his book onto a little table and getting up. “You cannot leave. You are in custody.” “So it seems,” said K. “And why?” he then asked. “We are not assigned to tell you that. Go to your room and wait. Proceedings have been set in motion, and you will learn everything at the proper time. I am going beyond my instructions in speaking to you so helpfully. But I hope no one hears it except Franz, and he himself is being friendly towards you against all regulations. If your luck holds as well as it did in the choice of your guards, you can be confident.” K. wanted to sit down, but now saw that there was nowhere to sit in the entire room except the chair by the window. “You'll come to see how true all this is,” said Franz, approaching him together with the other man. The latter in particular towered over K. and repeatedly patted him on the shoulder. Both examined K.'s nightshirt and said that he would now have to put on a much worse shirt, but that they would keep this one along with the rest of his linen and return it if his case turned out favourably. “You're better off giving these things to us than to the storeroom,” they said, “because there is often embezzlement at the storeroom, and besides, they sell everything there after a certain time, regardless of whether the proceedings concerned have ended or not. And cases like these do go on for so long, especially lately. Of course, you would eventually receive the proceeds from the storeroom, but first of all those proceeds are small to begin with, since a sale is decided by the size of the bribe, not the size of the bid, and then experience shows that such proceeds shrink as they pass from hand to hand and from year to year.” K. paid scarcely any attention to these speeches. He did not place much value on whatever right he might still have to dispose of his possessions; it mattered far more to him to understand his situation clearly; yet in these people's presence he could not even think, for the second guard's belly—guards were surely all they could be—kept bumping against him in an almost friendly way, while, when he looked up, he saw a dry, bony face, quite at odds with the heavy body, with a prominent nose bent to one side, communicating over his head with the other guard. What sort of people were these? What were they talking about? What authority did they belong to? After all, K. lived in a state governed by law, peace prevailed everywhere, all the laws remained in force; who dared to assault him in his own home? He always tended to take things as lightly as possible, to believe the worst only when the worst happened, to make no provision for the future even when everything looked threatening. But here that did not seem right to him. The whole thing could certainly be regarded as a joke, a crude joke his colleagues at the bank had arranged for some unknown reason, perhaps because today was his thirtieth birthday; that was of course possible, perhaps he merely needed to find some way of laughing in the guards' faces and they would laugh along, perhaps they were porters from the street corner, they did not look unlike them—nevertheless, this time, almost from his first sight of the guard Franz, he had been determined not to surrender the slightest advantage he might possess over these people. K. saw very little danger in anyone later saying he could not take a joke, but he did remember—although it was not otherwise his habit to learn from experience—a few incidents, insignificant in themselves, in which, unlike his friends, he had consciously behaved carelessly, without the slightest sense of the possible consequences, and had been punished by the outcome. It must not happen again, at least not this time; if this was a comedy, he would play his part.
about:
Josef K. wakes to find strangers taking charge of his room and his breakfast. They say he is under arrest, but let him go to work. No one tells him what he has done. His efforts to obtain an explanation draw him into hearings, offices and conversations in which every apparent source of help creates another uncertainty.

Kafka gives this extraordinary situation the texture of ordinary life: a missed breakfast, a crowded staircase, a neighbour disturbed at night, the pressure of work at a bank. K. argues, calculates and defends his standing. The narration stays close to him without settling whether his understanding of other people is reliable. The unease often arrives through comedy.

Written in 1914–1915 and left unfinished, the novel first appeared in 1925 in an edition arranged by Max Brod. This package follows the ten main chapters in a transcription of that first edition and uses neutral numbered labels. Its modern English is a fresh Tinct rendering directly from the German; there is no human English translation supplied as a comparison edition.

whyItMatters.title: An accusation without an explanation
whyItMatters.body: K. is expected to respond before he knows what he must answer. The novel makes that imbalance concrete through appointments, rooms and conversations, asking what a defence can mean when the terms of judgment remain unavailable.

whyItMatters.title: The authority we help to sustain
whyItMatters.body: K. resists the court, yet seeks its recognition, follows its leads and measures other people by their influence. His changing conduct lets readers examine how opposition and dependence can grow together.

whyItMatters.title: A voice that leaves judgment open
whyItMatters.body: The narration reports absurd arrangements with practical precision. It also follows K.’s quick conclusions closely enough to make them persuasive without guaranteeing that they are true. Reading means noticing the distance between what happens and what he believes it means.

angleCards.title: Who knows what?
angleCards.text: Track each claim about the court back to its speaker. Which claims rest on observation, which on hearsay, and which on K.’s own interpretation?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to distinguish events from claims about them and notice when an assumption starts being treated as knowledge.

angleCards.title: The comedy of procedure
angleCards.text: Watch the breakfast, clothing, furniture and timing. How do practical inconveniences make official power both ridiculous and effective?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the dry comedy of ordinary objects and routines without losing sight of the coercion they carry.

angleCards.title: Doors, rooms and permission
angleCards.text: Notice who may enter a room, who has to wait, and who listens from outside. The novel repeatedly turns access to private and public space into a question of authority.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to track thresholds and intrusions, including K.’s own treatment of other people’s boundaries.

angleCards.title: Reading an unfinished novel
angleCards.text: The ten-chapter sequence comes through Brod’s posthumous arrangement. Read the connections carefully while leaving room for breaks, uncertainties and questions the novel does not settle.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how the arranged sequence shapes my expectations without treating every unresolved detail as a puzzle with one final answer.

cast.name: Josef K.
cast.description: A senior bank employee who expects reason, status and professional competence to make his position clear. An unexplained arrest draws those expectations into question.

cast.name: Mrs Grubach
cast.description: K.’s landlady, whose concern for her lodgers includes close attention to their reputations. Her domestic judgments accompany the first official intrusion.

cast.name: Miss Bürstner
cast.description: A typist whose room is used during K.’s arrest. She listens to his account while insisting on her own time, space and responsibility.

cast.name: Franz and Willem
cast.description: The two men who take charge of K. on the morning of his arrest. They invoke regulations while making their own demands.

cast.name: The examining magistrate
cast.role: The official at the first hearing
cast.description: He presides over the crowded room where K. tries to turn his examination into a public challenge to the proceedings.

cast.name: K.’s uncle
cast.description: A relative from the country who takes an urgent interest in K.’s case and introduces him to a lawyer.

cast.name: Huld
cast.description: A lawyer approached through K.’s uncle. His account of defence work raises questions about access, influence and dependence.

cast.name: Leni
cast.description: A woman in the lawyer’s household who takes a close personal interest in K.

cast.name: Titorelli
cast.description: A painter with connections to the court, approached as a possible source of help.

cast.name: Block
cast.description: A merchant whose experience of the proceedings gives K. another perspective on seeking legal assistance.

cast.name: The priest
cast.description: A clergyman whose conversation with K. turns on how a story about access to the law can be understood.
